The user says (in French): "I would like to create a skill for all development on STM32". They likely want to define a new skill in the OpenCode system that provides instructions and resources for STM32 development. We need to create a skill definition perhaps as a skill file. In this environment, skills are defined elsewhere; but we can likely create a skill file under some directory like .opencode/skills/... Or perhaps we need to guide the user on how to create a skill.

We need to ask clarifying questions: what's the intended functionality? Could be they want a skill that offers guidance, commands for STM32 development, such as generating code, using CubeMX, etc. We may need to ask them specifics.

We should respond asking for details like what they'd like the skill to do, what commands/tools, environment specifics.

Thus, ask clarification.

**Création d’un skill “STM32” – premières étapes**

Pour vous aider à mettre en place un **skill** dédié au développement STM32, j’ai besoin de quelques précisions :

| Question | Pourquoi c’est utile |
|----------|----------------------|
| **Quel(s) problème(s) ou quelles tâches le skill doit‑il couvrir ?** (ex. : génération d’init‑code, configuration des periphériques, compilation, flash, debug, recherche d’exemples, etc.) | Cela détermine le **scope** du skill et les instructions à inclure. |
| **Quel(s) outil(s) ou chaîne(s) de compilation utilisez‑vous ?** (ARM‑GCC, Keil, IAR, STM32CubeIDE, Makefile, CMake, etc.) | Le skill pourra référencer les bonnes lignes de commande ou options de configuration. |
| **Souhaitez‑vous intégrer des actions automatisées (ex. : génération de projet, compilation, flash) via les outils d’OpenCode ?** | Si oui, on pourra ajouter des **sub‑agents** (ex. `subagent` : `execute`, `shell`) ou des **templates** de script. |
| **Y a‑t‑il des ressources particulières à inclure** ? (liens vers la documentation STM32, modèles de projet, scripts CubeMX, etc.) | Elles seront listées dans la section **Resources** du skill. |
| **Quel format de réponse préférez‑vous** ? (texte simple, markdown, tableau, exemples de code, etc.) | Le skill pourra formater les réponses pour être le plus lisible possible dans votre workflow. |
| **Voulez‑vous que le skill soit partagé (public) ou uniquement local à votre environnement ?** | Cela influence où le skill sera stocké (dans le répertoire du workspace ou dans un dépôt partagé). |

---

### Exemple de squelette de skill (à adapter)

```yaml
# .opencode/skills/stm32_dev.yaml
id: stm32_dev
name: STM32 Development Helper
description: |
  Un assistant pour toutes les étapes du développement STM32 :
  - Création de projets (CubeMX, Makefile, CMake)
  - Configuration des périphériques (GPIO, UART, SPI, I2C, …)
  - Compilation avec arm‑gcc / STM32CubeIDE
  - Flash et débogage (ST‑Link, J‑Link)
  - Recherche d’exemples et de documentation officielle

resources:
  - name: STM32CubeIDE documentation
    url: https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubeide.html
  - name: STM32 HAL library reference
    url: https://www.st.com/resource/en/reference_manual/dm00135183.pdf

commands:
  create_project:
    description: Génère un squelette de projet STM32 avec CubeMX ou un Makefile.
    parameters:
      - name: mcu
        type: string
        description: Nom du MCU (ex. : STM32F429ZI)
      - name: toolchain
        type: enum
        enum: [gcc, keil, iar, cubeide]
    script: |
      # Exemple (pseudo‑code) :
      #   cube-mx generate --mcu {{mcu}} --toolchain {{toolchain}} --output ./{{mcu}}_project
  compile:
    description: Compile le projet avec la chaîne sélectionnée.
    parameters:
      - name: project_path
        type: string
    script: |
      # Si toolchain = gcc
      make -C {{project_path}}
  flash:
    description: Flashe le firmware sur la carte via ST‑Link.
    parameters:
      - name: bin_path
        type: string
    script: |
      st-flash write {{bin_path}} 0x8000000
```

Vous n’avez pas besoin de coller le fichier complet maintenant ; une fois que vous aurez confirmé les points ci‑dessus, je pourrai :

1. **Créer le fichier de skill** dans le répertoire approprié de votre workspace.  
2. **Ajouter les templates / scripts** que vous avez validés.  
3. **Enregistrer le skill** avec la commande OpenCode correspondante (si vous avez besoin d’une commande spécifique).  

---

### Prochaine étape

Merci de répondre aux questions du tableau ; vous pouvez simplement cocher les cases qui vous conviennent ou ajouter des détails supplémentaires. Dès que nous aurons ces informations, je procéderai à la mise en place du skill.

id: stm32_dev
name: STM32 Development Helper
description: |
  Assistant skill for STM32 development covering project generation, compilation with STM32CubeIDE, documentation generation, project templating, flashing, COM‑port handling, test/config creation, author/version tracking, and peripheral documentation.

resources:
  - name: STM32CubeIDE documentation
    url: https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubeide.html
  - name: STM32 HAL library reference
    url: https://www.st.com/resource/en/reference_manual/dm00135183.pdf

commands:
  generate_project:
    description: Generate a new STM32 project using STM32CubeIDE (or CubeMX) based on a selected MCU and optional peripheral configuration.
    parameters:
      - name: mcu
        type: string
        description: MCU part number (e.g. STM32F429ZI).
      - name: project_name
        type: string
        description: Name of the project directory.
      - name: use_cubeide
        type: boolean
        description: Use STM32CubeIDE CLI if true, otherwise generate a Makefile template.
    script: |
      if {{use_cubeide}}:
        # STM32CubeIDE CLI (requires IDE installed and CLI path in %PATH%)
        stm32cubeide -nosplash -application org.eclipse.cdt.managedbuilder.core.headlessbuild -importAll {{project_name}} -import {{mcu}} || echo "Failed to import project"
      else:
        # Create a minimal Makefile template (placeholder)
        mkdir -p {{project_name}}/Src {{project_name}}/Inc
        cat > {{project_name}}/Makefile <<'EOF'
        CC=arm-none-eabi-gcc
        CFLAGS=-mcpu=cortex-m4 -mthumb -O2 -Wall
        SRC=$(wildcard Src/*.c)
        OBJ=$(SRC:.c=.o)
        all: firmware.elf
        firmware.elf: $(OBJ)
        	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -TSTM32F429ZI.ld -o $@ $^
        clean:
        	rm -f $(OBJ) firmware.elf
        EOF
  compile_project:
    description: Compile the STM32 project using the selected toolchain (STM32CubeIDE or Makefile).
    parameters:
      - name: project_path
        type: string
        description: Path to the project root.
      - name: use_cubeide
        type: boolean
        description: Use STM32CubeIDE build if true, otherwise call make.
    script: |
      if {{use_cubeide}}:
        stm32cubeide -nosplash -application org.eclipse.cdt.managedbuilder.core.headlessbuild -cleanBuild all {{project_path}}
      else:
        make -C {{project_path}}
  generate_docs:
    description: Generate project documentation with Doxygen.
    parameters:
      - name: project_path
        type: string
        description: Path to the project root.
    script: |
      cd {{project_path}}
      if [ ! -f Doxyfile ]; then
        doxygen -g Doxyfile
      fi
      doxygen Doxyfile
  version_template:
    description: Increment the project template version (semantic minor) and commit changes.
    parameters:
      - name: template_dir
        type: string
        description: Directory containing the template version file.
    script: |
      VERSION_FILE="{{template_dir}}/VERSION.txt"
      if [ -f $VERSION_FILE ]; then
        CURRENT=$(cat $VERSION_FILE)
        # Assume format 0.0x, increment last digit
        BASE=$(echo $CURRENT | cut -d. -f1)
        MINOR=$(echo $CURRENT | cut -d. -f2 | tr -d '0')
        NEW_MINOR=$((MINOR + 1))
        echo "${BASE}.0${NEW_MINOR}" > $VERSION_FILE
      else
        echo "0.01" > $VERSION_FILE
      fi
  flash_card:
    description: Flash the compiled binary onto the STM32 board using ST‑Link.
    parameters:
      - name: binary_path
        type: string
        description: Path to the .elf or .bin file.
    script: |
      st-flash write {{binary_path}} 0x8000000
  open_com_port:
    description: Open the board’s COM port for serial communication (e.g., for tests).
    parameters:
      - name: com_port
        type: string
        description: COM port identifier (e.g., COM3).
      - name: baud_rate
        type: integer
        description: Baud rate, default 115200.
    script: |
      # Using pyserial (assumes python in PATH)
      python - <<PY
import serial, sys, time
port = "{{com_port}}"
baud = {{baud_rate}}
ser = serial.Serial(port, baud, timeout=1)
print(f"Opened {port} at {baud} baud")
# Keep open for interactive session – replace with actual test logic
time.sleep(2)
ser.close()
PY
  create_test_file:
    description: Create a skeleton unit‑test file for a given peripheral.
    parameters:
      - name: peripheral
        type: string
        description: Name of the peripheral (e.g., sdcard, i2c1).
      - name: test_dir
        type: string
        description: Directory where the test file will be placed.
    script: |
      mkdir -p {{test_dir}}
      cat > {{test_dir}}/test_{{peripheral}}.c <<'EOF'
      /* Unit test for {{peripheral}} */
      #include "{{peripheral}}.h"
      #include <assert.h>

      void test_{{peripheral}}_init(void) {
        // TODO: implement test
        assert(1);
      }

      int main(void) {
        test_{{peripheral}}_init();
        return 0;
      }
      EOF
  create_config_file:
    description: Initialise a configuration JSON file with author and version information.
    parameters:
      - name: config_path
        type: string
        description: Path to the config file to create.
      - name: author
        type: string
        description: Author name.
      - name: version
        type: string
        description: Initial version string.
    script: |
      cat > {{config_path}} <<'EOF'
      {
        "author": "{{author}}",
        "version": "{{version}}",
        "created": "$(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
      }
      EOF
  init_documentation_structure:
    description: Initialise the shared documentation directory with peripheral sub‑folders and markdown templates.
    parameters:
      - name: doc_root
        type: string
        description: Root documentation directory (e.g., docs).
    script: |
      mkdir -p {{doc_root}}/peripherals
      touch {{doc_root}}/HISTORY.md {{doc_root}}/STEPS.md
      echo "# Project History\n\n*(auto‑generated)*" > {{doc_root}}/HISTORY.md
      echo "# Project Steps\n\n*(auto‑generated)*" > {{doc_root}}/STEPS.md
      # Example peripheral folder
      mkdir -p {{doc_root}}/peripherals/STM32F429ZI
      echo "# STM32F429ZI" > {{doc_root}}/peripherals/STM32F429ZI/README.md

# Agent Skills

Define reusable behavior via SKILL.md definitions

Agent skills let OpenCode discover reusable instructions from your repo or home directory. Skills are loaded on-demand via the native `skill` tool—agents see available skills and can load the full content when needed.

---

## [Place files](#place-files)

Create one folder per skill name and put a `SKILL.md` inside it. OpenCode searches these locations:

- Project config: `.opencode/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`

- Global config: `~/.config/opencode/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`

- Project Claude-compatible: `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`

- Global Claude-compatible: `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`

- Project agent-compatible: `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`

- Global agent-compatible: `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`

---

## [Understand discovery](#understand-discovery)

For project-local paths, OpenCode walks up from your current working directory until it reaches the git worktree. It loads any matching `skills/*/SKILL.md` in `.opencode/` and any matching `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` or `.agents/skills/*/SKILL.md` along the way.

Global definitions are also loaded from `~/.config/opencode/skills/*/SKILL.md`, `~/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md`, and `~/.agents/skills/*/SKILL.md`.

---

## [Write frontmatter](#write-frontmatter)

Each `SKILL.md` must start with YAML frontmatter. Use these Agent Skills fields:

- `name` (required)

- `description` (required)

- `license` (optional)

- `compatibility` (optional)

- `metadata` (optional, string-to-string map)

Unknown frontmatter fields are ignored. OpenCode 1 does not use metadata to control slash commands or automatic skill selection.

---

## [Validate names](#validate-names)

`name` must:

- Be 1–64 characters

- Be lowercase alphanumeric with single hyphen separators

- Not start or end with `-`

- Not contain consecutive `--`

- Match the directory name that contains `SKILL.md`

Equivalent regex:

```
^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$
```

---

## [Follow length rules](#follow-length-rules)

`description` must be 1-1024 characters. Keep it specific enough for the agent to choose correctly.

---

## [Use an example](#use-an-example)

Create `.opencode/skills/git-release/SKILL.md` like this:

~~~
---name: git-releasedescription: Create consistent releases and changelogslicense: MITcompatibility: opencodemetadata:  audience: maintainers  workflow: github---
## What I do
- Draft release notes from merged PRs- Propose a version bump- Provide a copy-pasteable `gh release create` command
## When to use me
Use this when you are preparing a tagged release.Ask clarifying questions if the target versioning scheme is unclear.
~~~

---

## [Recognize tool description](#recognize-tool-description)

OpenCode lists available skills in the `skill` tool description. Each entry includes the skill name and description:

```
<available_skills>  <skill>    <name>git-release</name>    <description>Create consistent releases and changelogs</description>  </skill></available_skills>
```

The agent loads a skill by calling the tool:

```
skill({ name: "git-release" })
```

---

## [Configure permissions](#configure-permissions)

Control which skills agents can access using pattern-based permissions in `opencode.json`:

```
{  "permission": {    "skill": {      "*": "allow",      "pr-review": "allow",      "internal-*": "deny",      "experimental-*": "ask"    }  }}
```

| Permission | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `allow` | Skill loads immediately |
| `deny` | Skill hidden from agent, access rejected |
| `ask` | User prompted for approval before loading |

Patterns support wildcards: `internal-*` matches `internal-docs`, `internal-tools`, etc.

---

## [Override per agent](#override-per-agent)

Give specific agents different permissions than the global defaults.

**For custom agents** (in agent frontmatter):

```
---permission:  skill:    "documents-*": "allow"---
```

**For built-in agents** (in `opencode.json`):

```
{  "agent": {    "plan": {      "permission": {        "skill": {          "internal-*": "allow"        }      }    }  }}
```

---

## [Disable the skill tool](#disable-the-skill-tool)

Completely disable skills for agents that shouldn’t use them:

**For custom agents**:

```
---tools:  skill: false---
```

**For built-in agents**:

```
{  "agent": {    "plan": {      "tools": {        "skill": false      }    }  }}
```

When disabled, the `<available_skills>` section is omitted entirely.

---

## [Troubleshoot loading](#troubleshoot-loading)

If a skill does not show up:

1. Verify `SKILL.md` is spelled in all caps

2. Check that frontmatter includes `name` and `description`

3. Ensure skill names are unique across all locations

4. Check permissions—skills with `deny` are hidden from agents

# Portable build for the F429_sdcard_sdio_ecran project.
# Works with the STM32CubeIDE GNU toolchain and with arm-none-eabi-gcc on Linux.
#
# Usage:
#   make -j
#   make flash
#   make clean

TARGET        := F429_sdcard_sdio_ecran
BUILD_DIR     := build
PREFIX        ?= arm-none-eabi-
CC            := $(PREFIX)gcc
AS            := $(PREFIX)gcc
OBJCOPY       := $(PREFIX)objcopy
SIZE          := $(PREFIX)size
PROGRAMMER    ?= STM32_Programmer_CLI.exe
LDSCRIPT      := STM32F429ZITX_FLASH.ld

CPU           := -mcpu=cortex-m4
FPU           := -mfpu=fpv4-sp-d16
FLOAT_ABI     := -mfloat-abi=hard
MCU           := $(CPU) -mthumb $(FPU) $(FLOAT_ABI)

C_DEFS        := -DUSE_HAL_DRIVER -DSTM32F429xx -DDEBUG
C_INCLUDES    := \
	-ICore/Inc \
	-IDrivers/STM32F4xx_HAL_Driver/Inc \
	-IDrivers/STM32F4xx_HAL_Driver/Inc/Legacy \
	-IDrivers/CMSIS/Device/ST/STM32F4xx/Include \
	-IDrivers/CMSIS/Include

OPT           := -O0 -g3
CFLAGS        := $(MCU) $(C_DEFS) $(C_INCLUDES) $(OPT) -std=gnu11 -Wall \
	-ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -fstack-usage -MMD -MP
ASFLAGS       := $(MCU) $(OPT) -Wall -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections
LDFLAGS       := $(MCU) -T$(LDSCRIPT) --specs=nosys.specs --specs=nano.specs \
	-Wl,-Map=$(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).map -Wl,--gc-sections -static \
	-Wl,--start-group -lc -lm -Wl,--end-group

VPATH         := Core/Src:Drivers/STM32F4xx_HAL_Driver/Src:Core/Startup

C_SOURCES     := $(wildcard Core/Src/*.c) \
                 $(wildcard Drivers/STM32F4xx_HAL_Driver/Src/*.c)
ASM_SOURCES   := Core/Startup/startup_stm32f429zitx.s

C_OBJECTS     := $(addprefix $(BUILD_DIR)/,$(notdir $(C_SOURCES:.c=.o)))
ASM_OBJECTS   := $(addprefix $(BUILD_DIR)/,$(notdir $(ASM_SOURCES:.s=.o)))
OBJECTS       := $(C_OBJECTS) $(ASM_OBJECTS)
DEPS          := $(OBJECTS:.o=.d)

ifeq ($(OS),Windows_NT)
MKDIR_BUILD   := if not exist "$(BUILD_DIR)" mkdir "$(BUILD_DIR)"
CLEAN_BUILD   := if exist "$(BUILD_DIR)" rmdir /S /Q "$(BUILD_DIR)"
else
MKDIR_BUILD   := mkdir -p $(BUILD_DIR)
CLEAN_BUILD   := rm -rf $(BUILD_DIR)
endif

.PHONY: all clean flash flash-bin size list

all: $(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).elf $(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).bin $(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).hex

$(BUILD_DIR):
	@$(MKDIR_BUILD)

$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o: %.c | $(BUILD_DIR)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o: %.s | $(BUILD_DIR)
	$(AS) -x assembler-with-cpp $(ASFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

$(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).elf: $(OBJECTS) $(LDSCRIPT) | $(BUILD_DIR)
	$(CC) $(OBJECTS) $(LDFLAGS) -o $@
	$(SIZE) $@

$(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).bin: $(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).elf
	$(OBJCOPY) -O binary $< $@

$(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).hex: $(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).elf
	$(OBJCOPY) -O ihex $< $@

flash: $(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).elf
	$(PROGRAMMER) -c port=SWD -w $< -v -rst

flash-bin: $(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).bin
	$(PROGRAMMER) -c port=SWD -w $< 0x08000000 -v -rst

size: $(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).elf
	$(SIZE) $<

list: $(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).elf
	$(PREFIX)objdump -h -S $< > $(BUILD_DIR)/$(TARGET).list

clean:
	@$(CLEAN_BUILD)

-include $(DEPS)

# Flash and serial test workflow

## What I do

- Program the board through ST-Link/SWD.
- Open `COM39` at `115200 8N1`.
- Verify the SD card presence protocol.
- Produce a repeatable smoke test after each build.

## When to use me

Use me after a successful build and whenever the SD card detection or the serial output changes.

## Flash the ELF

```powershell
.\scripts\flash.ps1
```

Equivalent command:

```powershell
& 'C:\Program Files\STMicroelectronics\STM32Cube\STM32CubeProgrammer\bin\STM32_Programmer_CLI.exe' `
  -c port=SWD `
  -w 'build\F429_sdcard_sdio_ecran.elf' `
  -v -rst
```

Flash a raw binary at the Flash base address:

```powershell
& 'C:\Program Files\STMicroelectronics\STM32Cube\STM32CubeProgrammer\bin\STM32_Programmer_CLI.exe' `
  -c port=SWD `
  -w 'build\F429_sdcard_sdio_ecran.bin' 0x08000000 `
  -v -rst
```

## Open COM39

```powershell
.\scripts\open_com.ps1 -Port COM39 -Baud 115200
```

Python alternative:

```powershell
python -m serial.tools.miniterm COM39 115200
```

> Close STM32CubeIDE serial consoles and any other terminal that already owns COM39 before opening it.

## SD card presence protocol

The firmware must emit one line per state change:

```text
SD:PRESENT
SD:REMOVED
SD:MOUNT_OK
SD:MOUNT_FAIL
SD:PART1_OK
SD:PART2_OK
```

Expected behavior:

1. Boot with no card: `SD:REMOVED`.
2. Insert a card: `SD:PRESENT`, then `SD:MOUNT_OK`, `SD:PART1_OK`, `SD:PART2_OK`.
3. Remove the card: `SD:REMOVED`.
4. Insert again: the same sequence repeats.

## Automated smoke test

```powershell
python .\tests\test_com39.py --port COM39 --baud 115200 --duration 20
```

The test reads lines from COM39 and checks the expected patterns. Run it while inserting and removing the card.

## Hardware notes

- The card-detect input is currently declared on `PA10` as `SD_CARD_DET`.
- `PA10` must be configured as an input with pull-up (active-low card-detect switch).
- `PA10` conflicts with `USART1_RX`. The serial log is therefore assumed to be **USART1 TX only on PA9** (or another UART after rewiring).
- If COM39 is not the ST-Link VCP, confirm the actual UART and pins before changing the firmware.

## Safety

- Confirm the ST-Link serial number and board before programming.
- Do not flash the `.bin` at the wrong address; use `0x08000000`.
- Do not open COM39 with two programs at the same time.

description: Integrate LVGL for the LTDC screen and FatFs for the SDIO card, including two partitions (4 GB + remaining space), card-detect handling on PA10, and COM39 status messages. Use when adding the display stack, the filesystem, or SD card presence detection.

# STM32 middleware: LVGL, FatFs, and SD card

## What I do

- Plan and integrate LVGL on the LTDC display.
- Plan and integrate FatFs on the SDIO card.
- Support two partitions: partition 1 = 4 GB, partition 2 = remaining space.
- Implement SD card presence detection and COM39 messages.

## When to use me

Use me for display rendering, file access, SD card mounting, partitioning, and insert/remove tests.

## Current hardware facts

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| Screen | LVGL over LTDC, RGB565 |
| SD interface | SDIO 4-bit: PC8..PC12, PD2 |
| Card detect | `PA10`, label `SD_CARD_DET` |
| COM port | `COM39`, 115200 8N1 |
| Board | `32F429IDISCOVERY` |

> **Important:** The current `.ioc` declares `PA10` as `GPIO_Output`. It must be changed to `GPIO_Input` with pull-up (active-low switch). If your card-detect signal is active-high, use pull-down instead. `PA10` is also `USART1_RX`; the serial log must therefore be TX-only on `PA9` or use another UART.

## SD card presence state machine

```text
BOOT
 ├─ read PA10
 │   ├─ card present (low) → PRINT SD:PRESENT → mount → PRINT SD:MOUNT_OK
 │   └─ card absent  (high) → PRINT SD:REMOVED
 └─ loop every 200 ms
     ├─ stable present → mount if not mounted
     ├─ stable absent  → unmount → PRINT SD:REMOVED
     └─ state changed  → debounce 200 ms
```

Expected serial output:

```text
SD:REMOVED
SD:PRESENT
SD:MOUNT_OK
SD:PART1_OK
SD:PART2_OK
SD:REMOVED
```

## FATFS integration

1. Copy the FatFs middleware from the STM32Cube F4 package:

```powershell
$src = 'C:\Users\tmangear\STM32Cube\Repository\STM32Cube_FW_F4_V1.27.1\Middlewares\Third_Party\FatFs'
$dst = 'Middlewares\Third_Party\FatFs'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $dst | Out-Null
Copy-Item -Recurse "$src\src" "$dst\src"
Copy-Item "$src\doc" "$dst\doc"
```

2. Add `Middlewares/Third_Party/FatFs/src` to the include paths and source list.
3. Create `ffconf.h` from `ffconf_template.h` and enable:

```c
#define FF_USE_LFN      2
#define FF_MAX_LFN      255
#define FF_USE_MKFS     0
#define FF_FS_EXFAT     1   /* only if the card is larger than 32 GB */
#define FF_VOLUMES      2   /* two logical drives: 0: and 1: */
```

4. Adapt the SD diskio layer from the STM32Cube template:

```text
Middlewares/Third_Party/FatFs/src/drivers/sd_diskio.c
Middlewares/Third_Party/FatFs/src/drivers/sd_diskio.h
```

The diskio must:

- use the global `hsd` handle,
- map `pdrv == 0` to partition 1,
- map `pdrv == 1` to partition 2,
- read the MBR partition table once at init,
- apply the partition start LBA before `HAL_SD_ReadBlocks` / `HAL_SD_WriteBlocks`.

5. Mount both volumes:

```c
FATFS fs0, fs1;
f_mount(&fs0, "0:", 1);
f_mount(&fs1, "1:", 1);
```

6. Report results on COM39:

```c
printf("SD:PART1_OK\r\n");
printf("SD:PART2_OK\r\n");
```

## Two-partition layout

Recommended layout for a card of at least 8 GB:

| Partition | Size | Filesystem | Label | FatFs drive |
|-----------|------|------------|-------|-------------|
| 1 | 4 GB (4096 MB) | FAT32 | `SDCARD` | `0:` |
| 2 | remaining space | FAT32 (≤32 GB) or exFAT (>32 GB) | `DATA` | `1:` |

Partitioning is destructive. Use `scripts/partition_sdcard.ps1` only after verifying the disk number with `diskpart` → `list disk`. The script prints the diskpart commands by default and only executes them with `-Execute`.

## LVGL integration

1. Add LVGL as a submodule or vendored copy:

```powershell
git submodule add https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl.git Middlewares/Third_Party/LVGL
```

2. Copy `lv_conf_template.h` to `lv_conf.h` and set:

```c
#define LV_COLOR_DEPTH 16
#define LV_MEM_CUSTOM 0
#define LV_MEM_SIZE (48U * 1024U)
#define LV_TICK_CUSTOM 1
#define LV_TICK_CUSTOM_INCLUDE "main.h"
#define LV_TICK_CUSTOM_SYS_TIME_EXPR (HAL_GetTick())
```

3. Implement the display driver:

- `flush_cb` copies the rendered area into the LTDC frame buffer.
- The frame buffer lives in SDRAM (for example `0xC0000000`) or in internal RAM for a small area.
- Call `lv_disp_flush_ready()` after the copy.
- Configure `LV_COLOR_DEPTH 16` for RGB565.
- Use `HAL_LTDC_SetWindowPosition` and `HAL_LTDC_SetWindowSize` if the panel resolution is smaller than the LTDC timing.

4. Call `lv_init()` and `lv_timer_handler()` from the main loop.
5. Feed `lv_tick_inc()` from a 1 ms timer or use `HAL_GetTick()`.

> The current LTDC initialization has zero-sized layers and a null frame buffer. LVGL cannot render until the panel resolution, timings, and frame-buffer address are confirmed.

## Suggested module layout

```text
App/
├─ Inc/
│  ├─ log_uart.h
│  ├─ sd_monitor.h
│  └─ lvgl_port.h
└─ Src/
   ├─ log_uart.c
   ├─ sd_monitor.c
   └─ lvgl_port.c
Middlewares/
└─ Third_Party/
   ├─ FatFs/
   └─ LVGL/
```

## Test sequence

1. Build and flash.
2. Open COM39 at 115200.
3. Boot without a card → expect `SD:REMOVED`.
4. Insert the card → expect `SD:PRESENT`, `SD:MOUNT_OK`, `SD:PART1_OK`, `SD:PART2_OK`.
5. Remove the card → expect `SD:REMOVED`.
6. Insert again → expect the same sequence.
7. Run `tests/test_com39.py` and record the result in `docs/TESTS.md`.

## Safety

- Never run `diskpart clean` on the wrong disk.
- Verify the SD card capacity before choosing FAT32 vs exFAT.
- Do not enable `FF_FS_EXFAT` unless the FatFs version supports it and the card needs it.
- Keep the LVGL frame buffer out of the stack.

# Git workflow for the STM32 project

## What I do

- Initialize and inspect the repository.
- Create focused commits with a clear convention.
- Create and merge branches for features and fixes.
- Tag validated versions (`v0.01`, `v0.02`, …).

## When to use me

Use me before and after each feature, test, build, or release. Never commit build artifacts or secrets.

## Repository state

This directory may not be a Git repository yet. Initialize it once:

```powershell
git init
git branch -M main
git add -A
git commit -m "chore: initial STM32 project snapshot"
```

Check the state:

```powershell
git status --short
git log --oneline --decorate -10
```

## Commit convention

```text
<type>(<scope>): <short imperative summary>
```

Types:

| Type | Use for |
|------|---------|
| `feat` | New feature (LVGL screen, FatFs mount, SD detection) |
| `fix` | Bug fix (pin mode, UART, timing) |
| `build` | Makefile, CI, toolchain |
| `docs` | Documentation, history, steps |
| `test` | Test scripts and results |
| `refactor` | Code restructuring without behavior change |
| `chore` | Repository maintenance |

Examples:

```text
feat(sd): emit SD:PRESENT and SD:REMOVED on COM39
fix(gpio): configure PA10 as input with pull-up
build(ci): add GitHub Actions firmware build
docs(sd): document the 4 GB + remaining-space layout
test(sd): add COM39 insert/remove smoke test
```

## Versioning and tags

- `VERSION` and `config/project.json` carry the current version.
- Validated versions are tagged:

```powershell
git tag -a v0.02 -m "Validated SD detection and FatFs mount"
git push origin main --tags
```

- Tag only after:
  1. build succeeds,
  2. flash succeeds,
  3. the smoke test passes,
  4. `docs/HISTORY.md` and `docs/TESTS.md` are updated.

## Branch strategy

```text
main                  stable, validated versions
feature/<name>        new feature
fix/<name>            bug fix
test/<name>           test-only work
docs/<name>           documentation-only work
```

Create and merge:

```powershell
git switch -c feature/lvgl-port
# work, commit
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature/lvgl-port
```

## Daily commands

```powershell
git status
git diff
git add <files>
git commit -m "feat(display): add LVGL flush callback"
git pull --rebase
git push origin main
```

## Submodules for LVGL and FatFs

```powershell
git submodule add https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl.git Middlewares/Third_Party/LVGL
git submodule update --init --recursive
git add .gitmodules Middlewares/Third_Party/LVGL
git commit -m "build(middleware): add LVGL submodule"
```

When cloning:

```powershell
git clone --recurse-submodules <url>
```

## .gitignore rules

Ignored:

- `build/`, `Debug/`, `Release/`
- `*.elf`, `*.bin`, `*.hex`, `*.map`, `*.list`
- `*.o`, `*.d`, `*.su`, `*.cyclo`
- `.settings/`, `.metadata/`, `*.launch`
- Python caches, logs, `.env`

Never ignore:

- `Core/`, `Drivers/`, `Middlewares/`
- `.opencode/skills/`
- `docs/`, `config/`, `tests/`, `scripts/`
- `.github/workflows/`

## Safety rules

- Never use `git push --force` on `main`.
- Never commit secrets, tokens, or `.env`.
- Never commit a `.elf` or `.bin` unless a release explicitly requires it.
- Verify `git status` before `git add -A`.
- If a generated file is already tracked, remove it from the index without deleting it:

```powershell
git rm --cached path/to/generated/file
```

## Changelog and release checklist

- [ ] `VERSION` and `config/project.json` updated.
- [ ] `docs/HISTORY.md` updated.
- [ ] `docs/STEPS.md` updated.
- [ ] `docs/TESTS.md` updated with the test result.
- [ ] Build and flash succeeded.
- [ ] Git tag created (`v0.0x`).
- [ ] Tag pushed.

## Serial / SD card smoke test

### Prerequisites

python -m pip install pyserial
```

### Run

```powershell
python .\tests\test_com39.py --port COM39 --baud 115200 --duration 20 `

3. Wait for `SD:PRESENT` / `SD:MOUNT_OK`.
4. Remove the card.
5. Wait for `SD:REMOVED`.

The script exits with code `0` only when all requested patterns were observed.

SD:PRESENT
SD:REMOVED
SD:MOUNT_OK
SD:MOUNT_FAIL
SD:PART1_OK
SD:PART2_OK

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""COM39 serial smoke test for the STM32 SD card presence protocol.

Reads lines from the board's virtual COM port and optionally checks that
expected markers are observed. Run it while inserting/removing the SD card.

Requires pyserial:
    python -m pip install pyserial
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

try:
    import serial
except ImportError as exc:  # pragma: no cover - dependency check
    raise SystemExit(
        "pyserial is required. Install it with: python -m pip install pyserial"
    ) from exc


DEFAULT_CONFIG = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "config" / "test_config.json"


def load_config(path: Path) -> dict:
    if path.exists():
        with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            return json.load(handle)
    return {}


def main() -> int:
    config = load_config(DEFAULT_CONFIG)

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Read and validate COM39 SD-card messages.")
    parser.add_argument("--port", default=config.get("port", "COM39"))
    parser.add_argument("--baud", type=int, default=config.get("baudrate", 115200))
    parser.add_argument("--duration", type=int, default=config.get("duration_seconds", 20))
    parser.add_argument("--log", default="")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--expect",
        action="append",
        default=config.get("expected_patterns", []),
        help="Expected substring; repeat for multiple patterns.",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()

    expected = list(dict.fromkeys(args.expect or []))
    seen_lines: list[str] = []
    deadline = time.monotonic() + args.duration

    print(f"Opening {args.port} at {args.baud} baud for {args.duration}s")
    if expected:
        print("Expected: " + ", ".join(expected))
    print("Insert/remove the SD card now...")

    try:
        with serial.Serial(args.port, args.baud, timeout=0.5) as port:
            while time.monotonic() < deadline:
                raw = port.readline()
                if not raw:
                    continue
                line = raw.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").strip()
                if not line:
                    continue
                stamp = time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
                output = f"{stamp} {line}"
                print(output)
                seen_lines.append(line)
    except serial.SerialException as exc:
        print(f"Serial error: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    if args.log:
        log_path = Path(args.log)
        log_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        log_path.write_text("\n".join(seen_lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

    if not seen_lines:
        print("FAIL: no serial lines received.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    missing = [pattern for pattern in expected if not any(pattern in line for line in seen_lines)]
    if missing:
        print("FAIL: missing patterns: " + ", ".join(missing), file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    print("PASS: all expected patterns observed.")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

## Card detect and serial

| Pin | Signal | Current mode | Required mode | Notes |
|-----|--------|--------------|---------------|-------|
| PA10 | `SD_CARD_DET` | GPIO output | GPIO input, pull-up | Active-low switch assumed; conflicts with `USART1_RX` |
| PA9 | `USART1_TX` (proposed) | not configured | AF7 push-pull | TX-only log to COM39 if the ST-Link VCP is USART1 |
| PA0 | `UART4_TX` (alternative) | free | AF8 | Alternative if COM39 is wired to UART4 |
| PA1 | `UART4_RX` (alternative) | free | AF8 | Alternative if COM39 is wired to UART4 |

## UART conflicts

The LTDC and SDIO assignments consume most UART pins:

| UART | TX pin | RX pin | Conflict |
|------|--------|--------|----------|
| USART1 | PA9 | PA10 | RX used by `SD_CARD_DET` |
| USART2 | PA2 | PA3 | PA3 used by LTDC_B5 |
| USART3 | PB10 | PB11 | Both used by LTDC_G4/G5 |
| UART4 | PA0 | PA1 | Free on this pinout |
| UART5 | PC12 | PD2 | Both used by SDIO |
| USART6 | PC6 | PC7 | Both used by LTDC_HSYNC/G6 |

> **Decision required:** confirm whether COM39 is the ST-Link VCP (USART1) or an external USB-UART adapter. If USART1 is used for TX only, PA9 is sufficient and PA10 can remain the card-detect input. If bidirectional serial is required, use UART4 on PA0/PA1 and rewire COM39.

| Item | Current value |
|------|---------------|
| SYSCLK source | HSI (16 MHz) |
| PLL | ON, but SYSCLK still HSI |
| AHB / APB1 / APB2 | 16 MHz / 16 MHz / 16 MHz |
| Flash latency | 0 WS |

The script finds `arm-none-eabi-gcc.exe` and `make.exe` under `C:\ST` and runs `make -j4`.

See the `stm32-build` skill. The portable Makefile is the recommended CI path because it uses only relative paths.

Workflow: `.github/workflows/build.yml`

It runs on push and pull request:

1. Checkout.
2. Install `gcc-arm-none-eabi`, `make`, and `binutils-arm-none-eabi`.
3. `make -j$(nproc)`.
4. Upload `build/F429_sdcard_sdio_ecran.elf`, `.bin`, `.hex`, and `.map` as artifacts.

A self-hosted runner can flash and run the serial smoke test:

```yaml
runs-on: [self-hosted, windows, stm32]
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - run: .\scripts\build_and_flash.ps1
  - run: python .\tests\test_com39.py --port COM39 --duration 20

- STM32CubeProgrammer installed,
- the board connected through ST-Link,
- COM39 free,
- a physical operator or fixture to insert/remove the SD card.

- Build artifacts are ignored by Git.
- Releases are tagged `v0.0x`.
- The GitHub release should attach the ELF/BIN/HEX produced by the workflow.

# SD card — SDIO + FatFs

## Hardware

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| Interface | SDIO 4-bit |
| Data pins | PC8 (D0), PC9 (D1), PC10 (D2), PC11 (D3) |
| Clock | PC12 (CK) |
| Command | PD2 (CMD) |
| Card detect | PA10 (`SD_CARD_DET`), **must be input with pull-up** |
| Pull-ups | Verify the module has 10 kΩ pull-ups on CMD and D0..D3 |

## Current configuration

- `MX_SDIO_SD_Init` sets `SDIO_BUS_WIDE_4B` and `HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation`.
- The SD clock divider is `0` in the `.ioc`; verify the resulting clock is within the card's capability.
- No FatFs middleware is present yet.
- `PA10` is currently configured as `GPIO_Output`; this is incorrect for a card-detect switch.

## Partitions

| Partition | Size | Filesystem | Label | FatFs drive |
|-----------|------|------------|-------|-------------|
| 1 | 4 GB | FAT32 | `SDCARD` | `0:` |
| 2 | remaining space | FAT32 (≤32 GB) or exFAT (>32 GB) | `DATA` | `1:` |

### Partitioning

Use `scripts/partition_sdcard.ps1`:

```powershell
# Dry run: print the diskpart script
.\scripts\partition_sdcard.ps1 -DiskNumber 2

# Apply after checking the disk number
.\scripts\partition_sdcard.ps1 -DiskNumber 2 -Execute
```

> `diskpart clean` erases the entire card. Verify the disk number with `diskpart` → `list disk` first.

## FatFs plan

1. Copy `ff.c`, `ff.h`, `ffconf.h`, `diskio.c`, `diskio.h`, `ff_gen_drv.c`, `ff_gen_drv.h`, `integer.h` into `Middlewares/Third_Party/FatFs/src`.
2. Add `sd_diskio.c`/`.h` adapted from the STM32Cube template.
3. Read the MBR at LBA 0 and store the start LBA and sector count of both partitions.
4. Map `pdrv = 0` to partition 1 and `pdrv = 1` to partition 2.
5. Apply the partition start LBA in `disk_read`/`disk_write`.
6. Mount:

   ```c
   FATFS fs0, fs1;
   f_mount(&fs0, "0:", 1);
   f_mount(&fs1, "1:", 1);
   ```

7. Report:

   ```text
   SD:MOUNT_OK
   SD:PART1_OK
   SD:PART2_OK
   ```

## Card presence

State machine:

```text
read PA10 (active low)
  low  → present
  high → absent
debounce 200 ms
on change:
  present → print SD:PRESENT, mount, print results
  absent  → unmount, print SD:REMOVED
```

## Test procedure

1. Flash the firmware.
2. Open COM39.
3. Boot without a card → `SD:REMOVED`.
4. Insert a card → `SD:PRESENT`, `SD:MOUNT_OK`, `SD:PART1_OK`, `SD:PART2_OK`.
5. Remove the card → `SD:REMOVED`.
6. Re-insert → same sequence.
7. Run `python tests/test_com39.py --port COM39`.

## Known issues

- `PA10` is currently an output.
- The second partition requires MBR-aware diskio.
- exFAT requires `FF_FS_EXFAT` and a FatFs version that supports it.
- SDIO pull-ups and signal integrity must be checked on the actual board.

# Added memory — SDRAM / external RAM

## Internal memory

| Region | Start | Size | Use |
|--------|-------|------|-----|
| Flash | `0x08000000` | 2048 KB | Code and constants |
| SRAM | `0x20000000` | 192 KB | Data, stack, heap |
| CCM RAM | `0x10000000` | 64 KB | Fast data (no DMA) |

## External SDRAM

The 32F429IDISCOVERY board provides an 8 MB SDRAM device connected to the FMC. The exact part and bank depend on the board revision.

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| Size | 8 MB (64 Mbit) |
| Interface | FMC SDRAM |
| Typical base | `0xC0000000` |
| Use | LVGL frame buffer, large buffers |

## Why it matters for LVGL

A 480 × 272 RGB565 frame buffer uses:

```text
480 × 272 × 2 = 261,120 bytes ≈ 255 KB
```

This does not fit in the 192 KB SRAM with the rest of the application. Put the LVGL frame buffer in SDRAM.

A double buffer doubles the requirement:

```text
2 × 255 KB ≈ 510 KB
```

The 8 MB SDRAM has enough room.

- [ ] Confirm the SDRAM part and FMC bank on the actual board.
- [ ] Add the FMC/SDRAM initialization from the BSP or CubeMX.

- [ ] Verify read/write with a memory test before using it for LVGL.
- [ ] Document the frame-buffer address in `docs/peripherals/ecran/README.md`.

## Safety

- Do not place the stack or heap in SDRAM before verifying the FMC timing.
- Do not assume the base address; check the board schematic.
- Keep DMA buffers in SRAM or CCM, not in SDRAM, unless the FMC/DMA path is validated.

# COM port — COM39

## Settings

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| Port | `COM39` |
| Baud rate | `115200` |
| Data bits | 8 |
| Parity | None |
| Stop bits | 1 |
| Flow control | None |

## UART mapping

> **Decision required:** COM39 is assumed to be the ST-Link virtual COM port. The STM32F429I-DISCOVERY VCP is typically USART1 (PA9 TX / PA10 RX), but `PA10` is already used by `SD_CARD_DET`.

Options:

1. **USART1 TX only on PA9** — send logs, no receive. `PA10` stays the card-detect input.
2. **UART4 on PA0/PA1** — move COM39 to UART4 and keep PA9/PA10 free.
3. **External USB-UART adapter** — connect its RX to the chosen MCU TX pin.

Do not configure `PA10` as `USART1_RX` while it is used for card detection.

## Firmware messages

| Message | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| `SD:PRESENT` | Card-detect input became active |
| `SD:REMOVED` | Card-detect input became inactive |
| `SD:MOUNT_OK` | FatFs mount succeeded |
| `SD:MOUNT_FAIL` | FatFs mount failed |
| `SD:PART1_OK` | Partition 1 (4 GB) mounted |
| `SD:PART2_OK` | Partition 2 (remaining space) mounted |

Each message is terminated by `\r\n`.

## Monitor

```powershell
.\scripts\open_com.ps1 -Port COM39 -Baud 115200
```

Filter only SD messages:

```powershell
.\scripts\monitor_sd.ps1 -Port COM39
```

Python:

```powershell
python -m serial.tools.miniterm COM39 115200
```

## Automated test

```powershell
python .\tests\test_com39.py --port COM39 --baud 115200 --duration 20 `
  --expect SD:PRESENT --expect SD:REMOVED
```

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Check |
|---------|-------|
| `Access is denied` when opening COM39 | Another terminal/CubeIDE console is using it |
| No output | UART pin mapping, TX pin, baud rate, ground |
| Garbage characters | Baud rate mismatch or wrong clock |
| Only RX works / no TX | TX pin not configured as AF7/AF8 |
| COM39 disappears | USB cable/ST-Link connection |

## Safety

- Never drive `PA10` as an output while it is connected to the ST-Link RX line.
- Confirm the UART instance before enabling the peripheral.

Hello SAgaz.1,

yes you are right. If you are interested to use ST-link virtual com port(VCP) for visualizing USART data. You should use USART1 on pins PA9 and PA10. Further for this you need to have correct configuration of the solder bridges SB11 and SB15. Here is bit difference in the default configuration between BOARD 32F429IDISCOVERY and board STM32F429I-DISC1. But in both cases when you are interested to have the USART1 connected STLINK the solder bridges should be in state ON. More information could be found in the user manual UM1670 chapter 6.3.3.

content.text:
Interesting! We got a rapid toggle: `SD:PRESENT`, `SD:REMOVED`, `SD:PRESENT`, `SD:REMOVED` within 45 ms, then 4 seconds later `SD:REMOVED`. This indicates the card-detect input is floating/noisy (or the card is not actually present, or the pin is not connected). The debounce logic should have prevented rapid toggles because it requires stable for 200 ms. But the messages appeared within 45 ms, meaning our debounce logic is flawed? Let's inspect.

`SD_Monitor_Init` sets stable_present = read, raw_last = stable, raw_change_ms = now, and prints `SD:PRESENT` if present. Then `SD_Monitor_Process` is called in the loop. If raw changes to present, it updates raw_last and raw_change_ms and returns. If raw stays present, after 200 ms it sets stable and prints `SD:PRESENT`. So rapid toggles shouldn't produce messages within 45 ms unless `SD_Monitor_Init` itself printed one and then the loop printed another after 200 ms? The timestamps: 10:20:46.481 PRESENT, .502 REMOVED, .514 PRESENT, .526 REMOVED, then 10:20:50.191 REMOVED. The first PRESENT likely from `SD_Monitor_Init` at boot. Then the loop reading raw changes rapidly? The debounce should wait 200 ms. But maybe `raw_change_ms` isn't reset properly? Let's think.

At init, `stable_present = read` (maybe 1), `raw_last = 1`, `raw_change_ms = now`. Prints PRESENT. Then process: raw = 0 (card removed?) != raw_last (1), so raw_last=0, raw_change_ms=now, return. Next process: raw=0, raw_last=0; if raw != stable (0 != 1) and now - raw_change_ms >= 200? Not yet; return. After 200 ms, would print REMOVED. But we see REMOVED 21 ms later. So maybe `HAL_GetTick()` is not incrementing as expected? Or `SD_Monitor_Process` is called very fast, but 21 ms is not 200. Wait, the timestamps are from the PC, not the board. The board's `HAL_GetTick()` might be stuck or wrap? At 16 MHz, SysTick should work. But 21 ms is less than 200 ms. Unless `SD_Monitor_Process` is not the source; maybe the board is resetting repeatedly? The `SD:PRESENT`/`SD:REMOVED` sequence could be from multiple boots due to reset toggles? The ST-Link reset? No.

Alternatively, the messages are from `SD_Monitor_Init` on multiple resets caused by the card detect pin? No.

Maybe the card-detect pin is floating and the `HAL_GPIO_ReadPin` returns alternating values; the debounce should still require 200 ms, but if the raw value alternates every few ms, it never stabilizes, so no messages should be emitted. But we see them. Perhaps the debounce logic has a bug: `raw_change_ms` is set when raw changes, but if raw changes back and forth rapidly, `raw` might equal `stable_present` at some point and trigger? Let's examine:
```
if (raw != raw_last) { raw_last=raw; raw_change_ms=now; return; }
if ((raw != stable_present) && ((now - raw_change_ms) >= 200)) { stable=raw; print; }
```
If `raw` is 1 at init (stable=1, raw_last=1). Then raw becomes 0: raw_last=0, raw_change_ms=now. Next raw becomes 1: raw_last=1, raw_change_ms=now. Next raw becomes 0: ... It should never satisfy `raw != stable` and 200 ms because raw_change_ms resets each change. But if the raw value is stable at 0 for 200 ms, it triggers. The timestamps show changes every ~20 ms, so not 200 ms. Could the board's `HAL_GetTick()` be running much faster than real time? If SysTick is configured incorrectly, maybe the tick increments every ~0.1 ms, so 200 ticks = 20 ms. The `SystemClock_Config` sets HSI 16 MHz and SysTick priority. HAL_Init configures SysTick with `HAL_InitTick(TICK_INT_PRIORITY)` using `HAL_RCC_GetHCLKFreq()`. The clock config might report 16 MHz, so tick = 1 ms. Should be correct. But maybe the actual clock is 16 MHz and the tick is 1 ms; okay.

Wait, the timestamps of consecutive messages: 46.481 -> .502 = 21 ms, .514 = 12 ms, .526 = 12 ms. The debounce is 200 ms, so impossible unless `HAL_GetTick()` is incrementing ~10x faster. Could the HSI actually be 160 MHz? No, HSI is 16 MHz. But maybe `SystemClock_Config` configures PLL to 96 MHz but then sets SYSCLK source to HSI (16 MHz). The `HAL_RCC_ClockConfig` with `FLASH_LATENCY_0` might fail? If it fails, `Error_Handler` loops. But it doesn't.

Maybe the multiple messages are not from debounce but from repeated resets. The `SD:PRESENT` at .481 then `SD:REMOVED` at .502: if the board resets, `SD_Monitor_Init` prints based on the pin state at boot. If the pin is floating, each reset could read a different state. Why would the board reset repeatedly? The ST-Link `-rst` we issued resets once. But maybe the board is browning out due to the SD card or LCD? Or the ST-Link reset is toggling? The timestamps show 4 messages in 45 ms, then no more until 4 seconds later. Could be the board booting multiple times due to a crash? ### Next

- Configure the UART used by COM39.
- Configure `PA10` as input with pull-up and implement debounced card detection.
- Add FatFs with an MBR-aware two-partition diskio layer.
- Add LVGL and the LTDC display port.

## 2026-10-28 — v0.02 — USART1 log and SD presence monitor

### Done

- Enabled `HAL_UART_MODULE_ENABLED` and added the USART1 HAL driver to the project.
- Added `MX_USART1_UART_Init()`: USART1 TX only on `PA9`, 115200 8N1.
- Added `App/Src/log_uart.c` and `App/Inc/log_uart.h`.
- Added `App/Src/sd_monitor.c` and `App/Inc/sd_monitor.h`.
- Changed `PA10` from `GPIO_Output` to `GPIO_Input` with pull-up in `main.c` and in the `.ioc`.
- Moved UART and SD-monitor initialization before SDIO init so a missing card cannot block the boot.
- Made SDIO initialization non-fatal and skipped it when the card is absent.
- Verified COM39 reception:
  - `SD:REMOVED` is received at 115200 8N1.
  - USART1 registers show `USART1EN`, `TE`, and the correct baud rate.
- Verified `PA10` card-detect input is read by the firmware.

### Findings

- COM39 is the ST-Link Virtual COM Port (VID 0483, PID 374B).
- The ST community reports that the VCP uses USART1 (PA9/PA10) and requires solder bridges SB11/SB15 on some boards.
- With the card reportedly present, the boot log showed rapid `SD:PRESENT` / `SD:REMOVED` transitions. This points to a floating/noisy card-detect input or a board reset during SDIO initialization.
- SDIO initialization was temporarily disabled to isolate the presence detection.
- The card-detect active level and wiring must be confirmed.

### Next

- Confirm the SD card detect wiring and active level.
- Re-enable SDIO initialization only after the card-detect behavior is stable.
- Implement FatFs and the two-partition diskio layer.
- Add LVGL and the LTDC display port.

# FatFs middleware

Source: STM32Cube F4 V1.27.1 / FatFs R0.12c.

## Status

- [x] FatFs source copied into `src/`.
- [x] `ffconf.h` created with two volumes and exFAT enabled.
- [ ] `sd_diskio.c` adapted to the project `hsd` handle.
- [ ] MBR parsing for two partitions.
- [ ] Mount `0:` and `1:`.
- [ ] Build integration (Makefile and STM32CubeIDE).

## Configuration

`ffconf.h` currently sets:

```c
#define _VOLUMES   2
#define _USE_LFN   3
#define _MAX_LFN   255
#define _FS_EXFAT  1
```

## Integration plan

1. Create `src/drivers/sd_diskio.c` and `sd_diskio.h`.
2. Implement `disk_initialize`, `disk_status`, `disk_read`, `disk_write`, `disk_ioctl`.
3. Read the MBR at LBA 0.
4. Store the start LBA and sector count of partition 1 and partition 2.
5. Map `pdrv = 0` to partition 1 and `pdrv = 1` to partition 2.
6. Add the FatFs sources and include paths to the build.
7. Mount both volumes and report the result on COM39.

## Do not

- Do not add FatFs to the build until `sd_diskio.c` is implemented; the generic `diskio.c` references RAM/USB disk drivers that are not present.
- Do not enable `_FS_EXFAT` unless the card is formatted exFAT and the Flash budget is acceptable.

input.oldString:
## UART mapping

> **Decision required:** COM39 is assumed to be the ST-Link virtual COM port. The STM32F429I-DISCOVERY VCP is typically USART1 (PA9 TX / PA10 RX), but `PA10` is already used by `SD_CARD_DET`.

Options:

1. **USART1 TX only on PA9** — send logs, no receive. `PA10` stays the card-detect input.
2. **UART4 on PA0/PA1** — move COM39 to UART4 and keep PA9/PA10 free.

Do not configure `PA10` as `USART1_RX` while it is used for card detection.
input.newString:
## UART mapping

COM39 is the ST-Link Virtual COM Port:

```text
Name: STMicroelectronics STLink Virtual COM Port (COM39)
USB VID/PID: 0483:374B
```

The VCP uses **USART1 TX on PA9**. This was verified: the firmware emits `SD:REMOVED` on COM39 at 115200 8N1.

`PA10` is `USART1_RX` on the MCU, but it is reserved for `SD_CARD_DET`. The current firmware therefore uses **USART1 TX only**. Do not enable USART1 RX while `PA10` is used for card detection.

Options if bidirectional serial is required:

1. Move `SD_CARD_DET` to another free GPIO and enable USART1 RX.
2. Use UART4 on PA0/PA1 and rewire the adapter.
3. Use an external USB-UART adapter on the chosen TX/RX pins.

The ST community notes that some boards require solder bridges SB11/SB15 to connect USART1 to the ST-Link VCP (UM1670 chapter 6.3.3).

content.text:
Now build with Makefile. It will compile LVGL. Potential issues:
- `lv_conf.h` guard `#if 1` works.
- The LVGL sources may include `lv_conf_internal.h` which uses `__has_include`; okay.
- `lv_font_montserrat_14.c` compiles.
- `src/extra/widgets` find includes all; okay.
- `src/extra/themes/default` may require `lv_theme_default.h`; present.
- `LV_USE_THEME_BASIC/MONO` enabled and sources compiled.
- `src/extra/layouts/flex/grid` compiled.
- `src/draw/sw` compiled.
- The default theme may reference `lv_font_montserrat_14`; included.
- `lv_conf.h` has `LV_USE_LOG 0`.
- The `lv_conf.h` `LV_MEM_SIZE` 48KB; okay.
- `LV_TICK_CUSTOM` includes `main.h`; when LVGL source includes `lv_conf.h`, it includes `main.h` which includes `stm32f4xx_hal.h`; fine.
- `LV_TICK_CUSTOM` macro `HAL_GetTick()` requires `stm32f4xx_hal.h`; main.h includes it. Good.
- `LV_COLOR_DEPTH 16`.
- The LVGL `lv_color_t` struct `full` field exists in v8.3; yes.

Let's build.

Add `src/extra/lv_extra.c` to `.cproject` source entries? The source entry `Middlewares/Third_Party/LVGL/src/extra/layouts/flex` doesn't include `src/extra/lv_extra.c`. We need to add a source entry for `Middlewares/Third_Party/LVGL/src/extra`? That would recursively compile all extra (libs, others) which may fail. Instead, add a single source entry for the **file**? Eclipse source entries expect folders. Could add `Middlewares/Third_Party/LVGL/src/extra` with `excluding` for libs/others, but complex. Alternatively, move `lv_extra.c` into a source folder that is already a source entry? Not ideal. Or add `src/extra` as a source entry and trust that the extra widgets/themes compile; but it will also compile `libs`/`others` and fail. We can use an Eclipse `excluding` attribute on the source entry to exclude `libs` and `others`. The `.cproject` supports `excluding="..."` on `<entry>`? I think the attribute is `excluding` on `sourceEntries` entries, e.g.:
```
<entry excluding="libs|others" flags="..." kind="sourcePath" name="Middlewares/Third_Party/LVGL/src/extra"/>
```
Not sure of syntax. Alternatively, we can copy `lv_extra.c` into `BSP` or `App/Src` (via a small wrapper) and compile it there. We can create `App/Src/lv_extra_init.c` that defines `lv_extra_init` with only flex/grid calls. But `lv_extra_init` is a global symbol; the LVGL `lv_obj.c` calls it. We can implement our own `lv_extra_init` in `App/Src/lv_extra_init.c`:

### Card-detect finding

`PA10` is configured as input with pull-up. The firmware reads it high both with the card inserted and with the card removed. This means either:

1. the card-detect switch is not wired to `PA10`,
2. the module has no card-detect switch,

### PC10 / LCD conflict

The official BSP and UM1670 show that **PC10 is `LCD_TFT R2`** on the 32F429IDISCOVERY board. SDIO 4-bit uses PC10 as `SDIO_D2`. This is a hardware conflict:

- SDIO 4-bit cannot be used with the on-board LCD.
- When SDIO initialization reconsidered PC10, the LCD image was corrupted and the firmware could hang.
- The current firmware uses **1-bit SDIO** (PC8 D0, PC12 CK, PD2 CMD) and leaves PC10 to the LTDC.
- `HAL_SD_MspDeInit` no longer de-initializes PC10.
- `SD_ENABLE_SDIO` is set to `0` in `App/Src/sd_monitor.c` until the module's D1/D2/D3 lines are disconnected and the 1-bit wiring is verified.

- the LVGL status screen remains stable,
- card insertion/removal only updates the presence label and sends `SD:PRESENT` / `SD:REMOVED`,
- no `SD:INIT_FAIL` is emitted.

After the hardware fix, set `SD_ENABLE_SDIO` to `1` and re-test `SD:INIT_OK`.

Je comprends votre frustration. Le problème n’est pas LVGL : **il y a un conflit matériel sur PC10**, et c’est ce qui a provoqué l’écran brouillé puis le blocage.

## Ce qui se passe réellement

Le BSP officiel et le manuel UM1670 confirment :

- **PC10 = LCD_TFT R2** pour l’écran 2,4″ intégré.
- Le SDIO **4 bits** utilise **PC10 = SDIO_D2**.

Donc les deux ne peuvent pas fonctionner ensemble. Quand le SDIO était initialisé, il reconfigurait PC10 et écrasait la ligne rouge de l’écran. En plus, après un `SD:INIT_FAIL`, `HAL_SD_MspDeInit` désinitialisait PC10, ce qui corrompait l’affichage et bloquait le système.

## Ce qui a été corrigé

- Le SDIO est passé en **mode 1 bit** : `PC8 = D0`, `PC12 = CK`, `PD2 = CMD`.
- `PC10` n’est plus configuré ni désinitialisé par le SDIO.
- Le SDIO est temporairement **désactivé** (`SD_ENABLE_SDIO 0` dans `App/Src/sd_monitor.c`) pour que l’écran reste stable.
- LVGL v8.3.11 est intégré et affiche la version + la présence carte.
- Le firmware actuellement flashé ne lance donc plus l’initialisation SDIO : il ne devrait plus y avoir de `SD:INIT_FAIL` ni de blocage à l’insertion.

## Ce qu’il faut faire côté matériel

1. **Débrancher D1, D2 et D3 du module SD** (surtout **D2 de PC10**). Garder uniquement :
   - `CLK` → **PC12**
   - `CMD` → **PD2**
   - `D0` → **PC8**
   - `3.3 V` et `GND`
2. Ajouter des **pull-ups 10 kΩ** entre `CMD`/`D0` et 3,3 V si le module n’en a pas.
3. Alimenter la carte avec une **alimentation 5 V externe** : le ST-Link donne seulement 2,91 V, ce qui est trop bas pour une carte SD.
4. Vérifier la détection carte sur **PA10** : le firmware la lit haute avec et sans carte, donc le switch n’est probablement pas câblé ou son niveau actif est inversé.

## Ensuite

Quand le câblage 1 bit est fait, ouvrir `App/Src/sd_monitor.c` et passer :

```c
#define SD_ENABLE_SDIO 1
```

Puis reconstruire et flasher. On devrait voir `SD:INIT_OK` au lieu de `SD:INIT_FAIL`.

Les documents ont été mis à jour : `docs/PINOUT.md`, `docs/peripherals/sdcard/README.md`, `docs/HISTORY.md`, et le skill `stm32-middleware`.

Si vous préférez éviter complètement ce conflit, on peut aussi passer la carte SD en **SPI** sur des broches libres. Mais le 1 bit est la solution la plus simple si le module le permet.

- VCP: USART1 PA9/PA10, SB11/SB15; default config on 32F429IDISCOVERY may be OFF (we saw table 6; need to read page 23). The user's COM39 works, so the bridges are likely ON or the board is DISC1.

The PDF confirms:
- Board has 2.4" QVGA 240x320 TFT LCD, ILI9341, RGB protocol. Not 640x480.
- Pin table: PC10 = DB12 / R2 / LCD-RGB. So PC10 is LCD R2. The manual confirms the conflict.
- PC11/PC12/PD2 are listed under Free I/O (the columns are hard to read, but PC11 112, PC12 113, PD2 116 are under "Free I/O" likely). PC10 is LCD-RGB. So 4-bit SDIO on PC10 conflicts.
- VCP: USART1 PA9/PA10, SB11/SB15; default on 32F429IDISCOVERY is OFF, but on DISC1 is ON. The board revision F429-C01 has SB11/SB15 ON. The user's board may be a newer revision with VCP enabled. Good.
- Power: flexible options; 3V power supply input/output. The Adafruit 4682 is 3V; the 2.91V reading may be okay but near the limit. The manual says ST-LINK/V2-B minimum application voltage 3V; 2.91V is slightly below, but the board runs. Not the main issue.
- The board has 256KB RAM (192+64 CCM), 2MB flash, 64Mbit SDRAM.

So the user's statement "dans cubemx le ltdc est en rgb565 (640x480)" conflicts with the manual. If they are using the on-board 2.4" LCD, the LTDC must be 240x320, not 640x480. The BSP 240x320 is correct. The garbled text was because we used the BSP 240x320 (which is correct) but perhaps the LTDC timing/ARGB vs RGB565; we then fixed with RGB565 and LVGL and it became visible but flickers. The flicker may be due to the custom RGB565 layer vs the BSP's expected ARGB8888? Wait, the BSP uses ARGB8888, but the on-board LCD is 262K colors (18-bit), not 16-bit. The manual says 262K colors = 18-bit. The user says CubeMX LTDC RGB565 (16-bit) works without problems; maybe the panel accepts 16-bit. The BSP uses ARGB8888 and should also work. The flicker might be due to the LTDC timing or the frame buffer/refresh.

The PDF reading is the user's request; we should report the key findings and correct the record:
- The on-board LCD is 240x320 QVGA, not 640x480. If they configured CubeMX at 640x480, that's for an external panel, not the on-board LCD. If they're using the on-board LCD, the 640x480 config is wrong.
- PC10 is LCD_R2 per the pin table; 4-bit SDIO D2 conflicts. This is not an opinion; it's in the manual.
- The board's VCP is USART1 PA9/PA10; SB11/SB15 default OFF on 32F429IDISCOVERY, ON on DISC1/revision C01. The user's COM39 works, so bridges are ON or board revision.

The user says: "ou 8go et plus ok, en dessous on verra plus tard." — "or 8GB and more OK, below we'll see later." So the partition plan should only support cards **8GB and above**; for smaller cards, we don't care for now. We should adjust the logic:

- If total < 8GB, mark unsupported / "card too small, support 8GB+ only" and don't compute partitions (or just print a message).
- The user says "8Go et plus ok, en dessous on verra plus tard" — so we should require at least 8GB. The total capacity of an "8GB" card is usually ~7.2-7.5 GiB (about 7,400 MB), not 8192 MB, because marketing uses decimal GB. If we require `total_mb >= 8192`, a marketed 8GB card may fail. We need to consider actual capacity. The `HAL_SD_GetCardInfo` returns binary MB (MiB) based on 512-byte blocks. A "8GB" card has 8,000,000,000 bytes ≈ 7629 MiB. So the threshold should be maybe **7,000 MB** or **7,500 MB** to accept 8GB cards. The user says 8GB and above; we should detect the marketed capacity class. We can use a threshold of **7000 MB** (or 7168 MB = 7GB) to accept 8GB cards while rejecting 4GB cards (~3.7GB = 3,700MB). A 4GB card is ~3,700MB; 8GB is ~7,400MB. A threshold of 7,000MB cleanly separates them. Or use 7,500MB; some 8GB cards might be 7,382MB, so 7,000 is safer. We can define `SD_MIN_TOTAL_MB 7000U` and comment "accepts marketed 8GB cards (~7.4GiB), rejects 4GB cards (~3.7GiB)".
- For total >= 7,000MB: part1 = 4096MB, part2 = total - 4096 - 1. For a 7,400MB card, part2 = 3,303MB. Good.

Error 16 = 0x10 = `SDMMC_ERROR_TX_UNDERRUN` (Transmit FIFO underrun). This occurs during write operations. The partition creation writes block 0 and fails with TX underrun; the speed test write also fails with TX underrun. Reads probably work (init succeeded). TX underrun on SDIO write often indicates:
- The SDIO clock is too fast for the card or the bus capacitance/wiring; at 4.8 MHz it shouldn't be too fast for 1-bit. But maybe the card/module is slow or the data line has signal integrity issues.
- The write operation uses `HAL_SD_WriteBlocks` with a 4KB buffer in internal SRAM; should be fine.
- The SDIO **TX underrun** can occur if the data FIFO is not fed fast enough by the CPU/DMA. With `HAL_SD_WriteBlocks` polling, the HAL writes data to the FIFO in a loop; at 4.8 MHz, the CPU should keep up. But the CPU is at 16 MHz, and the SDIO clock is 4.8 MHz; feeding the FIFO should be possible. However, the HAL's `HAL_SD_WriteBlocks` may use `SDIO_WriteFIFO` in a loop; if the APB2 clock is 16 MHz and SDIO clock 4.8 MHz, it should be okay.
- The card might be in a state where writes fail (write-protected, not initialized properly, or the SCR no wide bus indicates a clone card). Read works? We haven't tested read after write failure. The write test fails, but read may work. `SD:INIT_OK` and `SD:CARD` work, which involve reading CID/CSD/SCR.
- The partition creation writes block 0; if the card is write-protected (lock switch), TX underrun isn't typical; it would return a write-protect error. The Adafruit 4682 module might have a **write-protect switch**? Some microSD breakouts have a WP pin, but microSD cards don't have a physical write-protect switch (full-size SD do). The module might have a level shifter or a WP issue.
- Error 0x10 TX underrun can be caused by the **SDIO clock being too high** or the **data line not connected correctly**. At 4.8 MHz, it's low. But if D0 is connected through a long wire or no ground, signal integrity can cause underrun. The card can read but not write reliably.
- Another common cause: **the SDIO peripheral's data FIFO is not being fed because the CPU is halted/interrupted**, or the `HAL_SD_WriteBlocks` timeout is too short. But 10s/5s timeouts are plenty. TX underrun means the FIFO ran empty during a write; the HAL uses polling and should keep it fed. At 4.8 MHz, each 512-byte block takes ~1ms; the CPU can feed.
- The card might be a **fake/counterfeit** card with poor write performance. Lowering the clock further (e.g., `ClockDiv = 16` or 32 -> 2.67 or 1.4 MHz) may help. The user suggested lowering; we can lower to 1.5 MHz or 2.4 MHz. Let's try `ClockDiv = 16` -> 48/(16+2)=2.67 MHz, or `ClockDiv = 32` -> 1.41 MHz. For 1-bit, 2.67 MHz is safe. If writes still fail, try 1.4 MHz.
- The **SDIO clock source** might be 48 MHz; `ClockDiv=8` -> 4.8 MHz. The HAL's `HAL_SD_WriteBlocks` uses the configured clock. Lowering is easy.
- The **TX underrun** might also be caused by the **SDIO hardware flow control** or **DMA**. We use polling; no DMA. The HAL `HAL_SD_WriteBlocks` uses `SDIO_WriteFIFO` and polls; it should be okay. Maybe the CPU is too slow at 16 MHz and the loop overhead with 4KB buffer is too much? At 4.8 MHz, the FIFO needs one 32-bit word every ~0.83 µs; the CPU at 16 MHz has ~13 cycles per word. The HAL loop may not keep up if it does a lot of work per word. That's a real possibility! The HAL `HAL_SD_WriteBlocks` polling loop writes to the FIFO; with a 16 MHz CPU, the SDIO clock should be much lower (e.g., 1.5 MHz) to avoid TX underrun. The SDIO clock is 4.8 MHz, which may be too fast for a 16 MHz CPU with polling. Lowering the SDIO clock to 1.5-2.4 MHz should fix the underrun.
- Alternatively, increase the CPU clock to 180 MHz (PLL) would allow 4.8 MHz; but the current clock is 16 MHz HSI. Lowering the SDIO clock is easier.
- The user suggested lowering the SDIO frequency; let's set `ClockDiv = 32` (48/(32+2)=1.41 MHz) or `ClockDiv = 24` (1.85 MHz). For reliable writes at 16 MHz CPU, 1.4 MHz is safe. The speed test will show ~150 KB/s, but it will work.
- We can also use DMA for SDIO writes to avoid CPU feeding issues, but that requires DMA configuration and HAL DMA functions; more complex. Lowering the clock is fine.
- We should also add a retry mechanism or fallback: try `ClockDiv=8`, if write fails, re-init at `ClockDiv=32`? The card is already initialized; changing `hsd.Init.ClockDiv` and calling `HAL_SD_Init` again might work. But simpler: set `ClockDiv=32` fixed for now.
- Error 16 during partition creation (writing 1 block) at 4.8 MHz: even a single block write fails, which strongly suggests TX underrun due to CPU/SDIO clock ratio or signal integrity. Lowering to 1.4 MHz is likely to fix.
- The card's SCR says no wide-bus support, which is suspicious; maybe the card is an **SDSC** card or a clone. But 1-bit init works. Writes might still work at low speed.
- We can also check if the card is **write-protected**; error 16 isn't write-protect, but if the card is locked, `HAL_SD_WriteBlocks` might fail with a different error. The module may have a WP switch; check it.

Let's modify `sd_card.c`:
- Set `hsd.Init.ClockDiv = 32U;` (1.41 MHz) for reliability.
- Maybe add a retry: if `HAL_SD_WriteBlocks` fails with TX underrun, re-init at lower clock and retry? For now, fixed low clock.
- The user wants speed tests; at 1.4 MHz, speed ~150 KB/s. The test will show the real throughput. That's okay.
- We can also try `ClockDiv = 16` (2.67 MHz) first; if it fails, 32. Which one? The CPU is 16 MHz; 2.67 MHz might be okay. The HAL polling loop for SDIO writes at 2.67 MHz needs a word every 1.5 µs; at 16 MHz, 24 cycles per word; the HAL loop might be ~20-30 cycles, borderline. 1.41 MHz is safer. ## Description

Micro SD cards and microcontrollers go together like micro-peanutbutter-and-jelly: SD cards are inexpensive, durable, easy to find at any shop, come in many sizes and can plug into any computer using a common SD card reader. That makes them perfect for microcontroller storage and retrieval \- whether it's images, fonts, GIFs, audio files, or sensor logs.

Wiring up SD cards when you're starting out is super easy \- you just [pick up one of our SPI-to-SD breakout boards](https://www.adafruit.com/product/254), [wire it to an SPI port and a chip select pin and with a little library work you're reading and writing files](https://learn.adafruit.com/adafruit-micro-sd-breakout-board-card-tutorial). That's all good and great but you may eventually find that your SD card project is a little...slow. **Even with fast SPI ports, there's only one data pin, which can make it hard to stream large files fast.**

If you've hit that limit, this breakout is designed to help \- unlike our other adapter, it is not fixed for SPI usage, and can be used with SDIO hardware support. SDIO is a multi-pin data protocol (up to 4 data pins at once!) SDIO also tends to be able to be clocked faster than SPI. Of course, your speeds will vary depending on what microcontroller you hook it up to. When we used SDIO instead of SPI on CircuitPython with the [SAMD51 Grand Central](https://www.adafruit.com/product/4064), we got a speed increase of about double when reading data off the card.

**You will need to verify that your microntroller has SDIO support and you have SDIO firmware/library support as wel**l. SDIO is usually available on higher end chips, and you may need to use a specific pin set. You can *still* use this for SPI mode, but it does not have level shifters so it's not for use with 5V microcontrollers.

**For use with 3V power and logic microcontollers only!** The SDIO pins are bi-directional, and we've never seen a 5V microcontroller with SDIO, so there's no level shifting or power regulator.

Comes with a bit of header so you can use in a breadboard. Doesn't come with the micro SD card itself!

# Adafruit MicroSD SPI or SDIO Card Breakout Board

## Overview

![](https://cdn-learn.adafruit.com/assets/assets/000/093/587/medium800/adafruit_products_4682-01.jpg?1595961694)

Micro SD cards and microcontrollers go together like micro-peanutbutter-and-jelly: SD cards are inexpensive, durable, easy to find at any shop, come in many sizes and can plug into any computer using a common SD card reader. That makes them perfect for microcontroller storage and retrieval - whether it's images, fonts, GIFs, audio files, or sensor logs.

Wiring up SD cards when you're starting out is super easy - you just [pick up one of Adafruit's SPI-to-SD breakout boards](https://www.adafruit.com/product/254), [wire it to an SPI port and a chip select pin and with a little library work you're reading and writing files](https://learn.adafruit.com/adafruit-micro-sd-breakout-board-card-tutorial). That's all good and great but you may eventually find that your SD card project is a little...slow. **Even with fast SPI ports, there's only one data pin, which can make it hard to stream large files fast.**

If you've hit that limit, [this new breakout](https://www.adafruit.com/product/4682) is designed to help. Unlike previous adapters, it is not fixed for SPI usage, and can be used with SDIO hardware support. SDIO is a multi-pin data protocol (up to 4 data pins at once!) SDIO also tends to be able to be clocked faster than SPI. Of course, your speeds will vary depending on what microcontroller you hook it up to. When we used SDIO instead of SPI on CircuitPython with the [SAMD51 Grand Central](https://www.adafruit.com/product/4064), we got a speed increase of about 200% when reading data off the card

![](https://cdn-learn.adafruit.com/assets/assets/000/093/588/medium800/adafruit_products_4682-00.jpg?1595961732)

 **You will need to verify that your microcontroller has SDIO support and you have SDIO firmware/library support as wel** l. SDIO is usually available on higher end chips, and you may need to use some specific pins. You can _still_ use this for SPI mode, but it does not have level shifters, so it's not for use with 5V microcontrollers.

**For use with 3V power and logic microcontrollers only!** The SDIO pins are bi-directional, and we've never seen a 5V microcontroller with SDIO, so there's no level shifting or power regulator.

The breakout comes with a bit of header so you can use in a breadboard. It doesn't come with the micro SD card itself!

![](https://cdn-learn.adafruit.com/assets/assets/000/093/601/medium800/adafruit_products_4682-03.jpg?1596049568)

[Secure Digital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secure_Digital), or SD, cards and tiny microSD cards are an inexpensive and ubiquituous means of adding lots of storage to devices. For a few dollars you can have gigabytes of storage at your fingertips (smaller than your fingertips actually!). With CircuitPython boards you typically have a very limited amount of flash memory to store code and data.

Wouldn't it be nice if you could connect a microSD card to a Python board and expand its storage?  It turns you can use microSD cards with CircuitPython! In fact some boards like the Metro M4 Grand Central come with microSD card support built-in, and for other boards like the Feather M4 Express family they can easily be connected to a microSD card that expands their storage.

![](https://cdn-learn.adafruit.com/assets/assets/000/093/602/medium800/adafruit_products_4682-02.jpg?1596049600)

WIth the Adafruit MicroSD SPI or SDIO Card Breakout Board, you can add an SD card to your project using the common SPI interface or the higher performance SDIO interface.

This guide also shows how to use a microSD card to store files for a CircuitPython board. Specifically using  a microSD card with CircuitPython boards like Feather M0 Adalogger, Grand Central M4, ItsyBitsy M4, and others will be covered in this guide. You'll learn how to connect a microSD card to the board and mount it as a new filesystem that store code & data.

Starting with CircuitPython 6, there are two new modules to improve the performance of SD cards using SDIO.

# Adafruit MicroSD SPI or SDIO Card Breakout Board

## Pinouts

![](https://cdn-learn.adafruit.com/assets/assets/000/093/589/medium800/adafruit_products_4682-04-crop.jpg?1595962579)

 **Power Pins**

- **3V** - This is the power pin. MicroSD cards must use 3.3V, so take care to only hook 3.3V to this pin. Hooking 5V or VBAT to this pin will damage your microSD card.
- **GND** - common ground for power and logic.

**Common Logic Pins**

- **DET** - Detect whether a microSD card is inserted.  This pin is connected to **GND** internally when there's no card, but when one is inserted it is pulled up to **3V** with a 4.7kΩ resistor.  That means that when the pin's logic level is **False** there's no card and when it's **True** there is.

**SPI Logic Pins**

If you're using SPI to connect to your SD cards, the pins have the following functions:

- **CLK** - This is the SPI **Cl** oc **k** pin / **SCK S** erial **C** loc **k** , and is an input to the SD card.
- **SO** - this is the **S** erial **O** ut / **M** icrocontroller **I** n **S** erial **O** ut pin, for data sent from the SD card to your processor.
- **SI** - this is the **S** erial **I** n / **M** icrocontroller **O** ut **S** erial **I** n pin, for data sent from your processor to the SD card. Its an input to the chip and can use 3V logic only.
- **CS** - this is the **C** hip **S** elect pin, drop it low to start an SPI transaction. Its an input to the chip and can use 3V logic only.

Pull ups are provided on all SPI logic pins.

**SDIO Logic Pins**

If you're using SDIO to connect to your SD cards, the pins have the following functions:

- **CLK** - The SDIO clock pin. A clock signal is sent by the microcontroller to the SD card on this pin.
- **CMD** - A bidirectional pin for communication between the microcontroller and the SD card, used for commands and information.
- **4 Data pins** - Four bidirectional pins for communication between the microcontroller and the SD card, used for transferring bulk data. Take care to wire these in the correct order!  The silk screen legends read:  **D0** , **D1** , **DAT2** , **D3**.

Pull ups are provided on all SDIO logic pins.

Note that when inserted, the SD card extends slightly beyond the edge of the PCB.  Check out the mechanical drawing on the [Downloads page](https://learn.adafruit.com/adafruit-microsd-spi-sdio/downloads).
